confirmed: The full markdown was read through its end and the full PDF checked, including the end figures; the source is the 21-page Research Square v1 posted October 2, 2025, DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-7743384/v1, by Liang Cheng, with the title recorded in the form (p. 1; figures on pp. 17-21).

The methods explicitly state random assignment of students to experimental and control groups, while also describing a quasi-experimental design and two natural classes; the form correctly preserves that unresolved allocation ambiguity (p. 7, section 3.2).

The classroom instructional experiment supports field_rct and has_randomized_people_study=true for two-screener routing: generative-AI assistance is assigned and creativity is scored on student texts (p. 7, section 3.2; p. 12, section 5.2.1).

The target sample is 60 first-year non-English-major university students, with assignment described as 30 per group; these are student counts, distinct from the two teacher instructors/interviewees and the AI technical staff member (p. 7, section 3.2).

The analyzed participant count and exclusions are not reported, so the overall and arm-specific n_analyzed fields appropriately remain null; neither at least 50 nor fewer than 50 analyzed people can be confirmed (p. 7, section 3.2; pp. 11-15, results and limitations).
Table 5 explicitly labels its N as 30 works analyzed, not 30 people; it cannot supply the analyzed sample size for the classroom experiment (p. 13, Table 5).

The experimental instruction uses ChatGPT, Midjourney, and DALL?E, whereas control instruction uses traditional teacher-assigned writing and manual correction; the intervention lasts eight weeks, 16 sessions, two per week (p. 7, sections 3.2-3.3; p. 8, section 3.3.2).

Writing-task evaluations use dual teacher scoring with AI cross-validation, and the creativity results explicitly concern scored AI-assisted texts; expert_raters and scored_on_output=true are supported (p. 8, section 3.4; p. 12, section 5.2.1).
Composite Pretest Mean 5.5, Posttest Mean 7.0, and Improvement Rate +27.3% exactly match the reported string and one-line finding (p. 12, Table 4, Composite row).
Originality Pretest Mean 5.3, Posttest Mean 6.9, and Improvement Rate +30.2% exactly match the reported string (p. 12, Table 4, Originality row).
Flexibility Pretest Mean 5.5, Posttest Mean 7.1, and Improvement Rate +29.1% exactly match the reported string (p. 12, Table 4, Flexibility row).

The conclusion separately reports creativity rising from 3.4 to 4.6 out of 5, without explaining its relationship to Table 4; the form correctly records this discrepancy (p. 14, section 6.1; p. 12, Table 4).

The creativity results provide pre/post means but no treatment-versus-control creativity estimate, analyzed Ns, standard deviations, standard errors, confidence intervals, or test results; the form does not overstate these as a between-group effect (p. 12, section 5.2.1 and Table 4; p. 17, Figure 2; p. 14, section 6.1).

The main instructional study is not a synthesis or a study consisting solely of AI-versus-human output comparisons, so context_class=none is appropriate for that study; the separate student-image/AI-image comparison in Table 5 is not a randomized classroom-arm creativity contrast (p. 7, section 3.2; p. 13, section 5.2.2 and Table 5).
No supplementary appendix or separate supplement is identified in the document; the end material consists of references and figures, consistent with source.supplement.exists=not_stated (pp. 15-21).
summary: The paper explicitly reports randomized AI assistance with creativity scored on students’ texts, so it belongs in the two-screener pipeline despite ambiguous natural-class wording and an unreported analyzed participant count. The existing reported numbers and source version are correct, but the form omits Table 4’s elaboration and fluency outcomes.
